title: Same format — same reliability?
text: Law student prepping for the bar needs volume, hundreds of practice questions in the exact style of the real exam, each with a worked explanation. Ask Claude for a batch and it writes them in minutes, a fact pattern, four answer choices, an explanation for why the right one wins. It reads exactly like a real bar question. The easy assumption, if reads like the real thing. The rule stated inside it must be as reliable as a certified bar review company's rule statement. title: The anchor — drafted, not pulled from a bank
text: Happening. Claude drafts the question from the general patterns of legal writing. It's learned how a bar exam fact pattern reads, how a plausible wrong answer sounds, not from a live license question bank that a bar review company keeps current against real statutes and cases. title: Style proves nothing either way
text: Hearsay question reads perfectly confident, polished, exam-shaped. That confidence is not the same as verification. The rule it states could be blended with a different exception or built on a since superseded standard and nothing in the pros would show it. And the reverse is just as true, an explanation that hedges, that says this may depend on jurisdiction, isn't a sign the rule is wrong, either. Confidence and hedging are both just style. title: Your turn
text: Read it with me. Ask Claude for practice bar question on a topic you're studying along with its explanation. Then ask a second question, which specific rule, case, or statute is this explanation relying on and could that vary by jurisdiction or have changed recently, check that citation yourself before you trust the rule.
